unstaged.title: Discard Uncommitted Edits in Working Tree
unstaged.workLostText: ⚠️ Yes, if you run git restore on uncommitted files. Any edits on your disk that were never staged or committed will be permanently overwritten.
unstaged.desc: You edited a tracked file on disk, but have NOT added it to staging. You want to wipe those edits and return to the last commit.
unstaged.code:
# Discard unstaged edits in a specific file:
git restore <filename>

# Or discard all unstaged edits in current directory:
git restore .
unstaged.effect: Permanently overwrites your working file on disk with the version recorded in HEAD/index.
unstaged.verify: Run git status. The file will no longer be listed under "Changes not staged for commit".
unstaged.warning: PERMANENT LOSS WARNING: Uncommitted working-tree edits cannot be recovered once discarded by Git.

staged.title: Unstage Files (Remove from Cart) Without Losing Edits
staged.workLostText: 🟢 No! git restore --staged only removes files from the staging index (cart). Your file edits on disk remain 100% intact and untouched.
staged.desc: You ran git add, but you are not ready to commit this file yet. You want to preserve your code edits in the file.
staged.code:
# Unstage a specific file:
git restore --staged <filename>

# Or unstage everything:
git restore --staged .
staged.effect: Removes the file snapshot from the staging index. Your working code edits on disk remain 100% untouched.
staged.verify: Run git status. The file moves from green (Changes to be committed) to red (Changes not staged).
staged.warning: Safe operation: Does NOT delete your code.

local-commit.title: Rewind or Amend a Local Commit (Not Pushed)
local-commit.workLostText: 🟢 No! git reset --soft moves your local branch bookmark backwards but keeps all of your code changes staged and ready in the cart.
local-commit.desc: You committed too early or forgot a file, but you have NOT pushed to GitHub yet.
local-commit.code:
# Option A: Rewind 1 commit and keep changes staged in cart:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Option B: Add a forgotten file to the previous commit:
git add <forgotten-file>
git commit --amend --no-edit
local-commit.effect: Moves HEAD back one commit while keeping your staged code ready to edit and re-commit.
local-commit.verify: Run git status and git log -1 to inspect the adjusted commit history.
local-commit.warning: Safe for local-only commits. Never rewrite commits already pushed to shared team branches.

pushed-commit.title: Undo a Public Commit on GitHub (Safe Inverse Commit)
pushed-commit.workLostText: 🟢 No! git revert creates a brand-new opposite commit without erasing or rewriting any history. Both the mistake and the fix are preserved.
pushed-commit.desc: The faulty commit has already been pushed to GitHub. Rewriting history with reset would break teammates' branches.
pushed-commit.code:
# 1. Find the commit hash to undo:
git log -n 5 --oneline

# 2. Create a safe inverse commit:
git revert <commit-id>

# 3. Push the revert to GitHub:
git push origin main
pushed-commit.effect: Creates a NEW commit that applies the exact opposite changes. History remains forward-moving and clean.
pushed-commit.verify: Run git log -1 to see the new revert commit, then push to upstream.
pushed-commit.warning: Team Standard: git revert is the approved way to fix public bugs without causing merge conflicts.

lost-reflog.title: Resurrect a Lost Commit or Deleted Branch via Reflog
lost-reflog.workLostText: 🟢 No! Git never immediately erases orphaned commits. They remain safely stored in your local reflog ledger for 30 to 90 days.
lost-reflog.desc: You accidentally ran reset --hard, deleted a branch with unmerged work, or lost a detached commit.
lost-reflog.code:
# 1. View your chronological local action ledger:
git reflog -n 15

# 2. Locate the commit hash before the mistake (e.g. HEAD@{2})
# 3. Create a rescue branch attached to that commit:
git switch -c rescue-branch HEAD@{2}
lost-reflog.effect: Recovers unreachable commits before Git's automatic garbage collection prunes them (retained locally for 30-90 days).
lost-reflog.verify: Run git log -1 rescue-branch to verify your recovered work is intact.
lost-reflog.warning: Local Ledger: The reflog tracks where HEAD has pointed on this computer.

protected-branch.title: GitHub: Protected Branch Update Failed (GH006 / Rule Violation)
protected-branch.desc: GitHub branch protection rules prevent direct pushes to main/master without an approved Pull Request.
protected-branch.code:
# 1. Package your commits into a new feature branch:
git switch -c feature/my-fix

# 2. Push the new branch to GitHub:
git push -u origin feature/my-fix

# 3. Open Pull Request on GitHub:
# Use the URL printed in terminal, or run GitHub CLI:
gh pr create --fill

# 4. Safely sync your local main back to remote clean state:
git switch main
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
protected-branch.effect: Moves your committed changes safely onto a branch and prepares a Pull Request for team review.
protected-branch.verify: Run git status on both branches to verify main is clean and feature/my-fix is published.
protected-branch.gotcha: GitHub Rule: Never force-push (--force) to a protected branch. The proper team path is always branch → Pull Request → merge.

auth.title: GitHub: Personal Access Tokens (PAT), SSH & Credential Caching
auth.desc: GitHub removed account password authentication in 2021. Pushing requires a Personal Access Token or SSH key.
auth.code:
# Option A: Authenticate cleanly via GitHub CLI (recommended):
gh auth login

# Option B: Clear cached stale credentials in Git Credential Manager:
git credential reject
# (Enter: protocol=https, host=github.com, then press enter on empty line)

# Option C: Test your SSH key connection:
ssh -T git@github.com
auth.effect: Resets invalid cached passwords in Windows Credential Manager / macOS Keychain and verifies access.
auth.verify: If SSH is working, GitHub prints: "Hi username! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access."
auth.gotcha: Fine-Grained PAT Caveat: Fine-grained tokens cannot push changes to .github/workflows/*.yml files. If editing workflows, use a Classic PAT with the workflow scope.

secret.title: GitHub: Push Protection Blocked Secret (GH013)
secret.desc: GitHub Secret Scanning detected a private key, API token, or credential embedded inside your commit history.
secret.code:
# 1. Rewind the commit while keeping file edits on disk:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# 2. Move sensitive secrets into a .env file and add to .gitignore:
echo ".env" >> .gitignore

# 3. Re-commit clean files and push:
git add .gitignore <cleaned-files>
git commit -m "fix: remove sensitive secret"
git push origin <branch>
secret.effect: Strips the secret from Git commit objects before they ever touch GitHub servers.
secret.verify: Push succeeds without GH013 pre-receive hook rejection.
secret.gotcha: False Positive? If the secret is a dummy test token, GitHub prints an unblock URL in the terminal output. Visit that URL in your browser to grant a one-time push bypass.

fork.title: GitHub: Sync Fork with Upstream Original Project
fork.desc: Your fork is behind the original repository and you need to incorporate incoming upstream changes.
fork.code:
# 1. Check your remotes (make sure upstream exists):
git remote -v

# 2. Add the original repository as "upstream" if missing:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/repo.git

# 3. Fetch latest upstream commits and merge linearly:
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main

# 4. Push updated main to your personal fork:
git push origin main
fork.effect: Brings your fork up to date with the parent repository without creating merge divergence.
fork.verify: Run git log -1 to verify your local main matches upstream/main.
fork.gotcha: Web Shortcut: You can also click the "Sync fork" button on your GitHub repository page, then run git pull locally.

protected-branch.title: GitLab: You are not allowed to push code to protected branches
protected-branch.desc: GitLab project settings restrict direct pushes to protected branches (usually main or develop).
protected-branch.code:
# 1. Create a feature branch with your commits:
git switch -c feature/my-fix

# 2. Push with GitLab push option to automatically open a Merge Request:
git push -u -o merge_request.create origin feature/my-fix

# 3. Re-align local main with remote:
git switch main
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
protected-branch.effect: Publishes your work to GitLab and auto-generates a Merge Request in one command.
protected-branch.verify: Check GitLab project web UI or follow the MR URL printed in terminal.
protected-branch.gotcha: GitLab Push Options: The -o merge_request.create flag is a native GitLab feature that creates the MR directly from your terminal!

auth.title: GitLab: Personal Access Tokens & SSH Alternative Port 443
auth.desc: Authenticating with GitLab over HTTPS requires a PAT with proper scopes, or SSH key.
auth.code:
# Option A: Authenticate using official GitLab CLI:
glab auth login

# Option B: Verify SSH key connection over default port 22:
ssh -T git@gitlab.com

# Option C: If corporate firewall blocks port 22, use alternative port 443:
ssh -T -p 443 git@altssh.gitlab.com
auth.effect: Bypasses firewall restrictions and establishes authenticated SSH or token sessions.
auth.gotcha: Token Scope: When creating a GitLab PAT, make sure to check write_repository. Deploy tokens without write scope will fail silently with 403 Forbidden.

secret.title: GitLab: Push Rules Secret Detection Blocked
secret.desc: GitLab Push Rules blocked your commit because it contains forbidden filenames or potential credentials.
secret.code:
# 1. Soft-reset to preserve code edits:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# 2. Remove the secret and add config to .gitignore:
git rm --cached <sensitive-file>
git commit -m "fix: sanitize configuration"
git push origin <branch>
secret.effect: Removes the forbidden credentials from Git index and history.
secret.verify: Push completes successfully without pre-receive rejection.
secret.gotcha: Enterprise GitLab: Self-hosted GitLab instances often enforce custom pre-receive regex checks for author email or issue reference IDs.

fork.title: GitLab: Sync Fork with Upstream Project
fork.desc: Keep your GitLab subgroup or user fork synchronized with the upstream group project.
fork.code:
# 1. Add upstream group remote:
git remote add upstream https://gitlab.com/upstream-group/repo.git

# 2. Fetch and merge:
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main

# 3. Publish to your fork:
git push origin main
fork.effect: Incorporates upstream MRs and commits into your local and remote fork repository.
fork.verify: GitLab project overview shows "This branch is up to date with upstream/main".
fork.gotcha: GitLab Mirroring: GitLab Premium/Ultimate supports automated pull mirroring in Settings → Repository → Mirroring.

protected-branch.title: Bitbucket: Branch cannot be updated directly (Branch Permissions)
protected-branch.desc: Bitbucket repository branch permissions restrict direct commits to main.
protected-branch.code:
# 1. Branch your work into a feature branch:
git switch -c feature/my-fix

# 2. Push to Bitbucket:
git push -u origin feature/my-fix

# 3. Open Pull Request:
# Navigate to your Bitbucket repository -> "Pull requests" -> "Create pull request"

# 4. Clean local main:
git switch main
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
protected-branch.effect: Stores your commits safely on a named branch and prepares a peer review Pull Request.
protected-branch.verify: Run git status. Local main is clean and up to date with origin/main.
protected-branch.gotcha: Jira Integration: Include your Jira issue key in the branch name (e.g. feature/PROJ-123-login) to automatically link PR status into Jira!

auth.title: Bitbucket: App Passwords & Atlassian Account Email Gotcha
auth.desc: Bitbucket Cloud deprecated account passwords for Git operations. You must use an App Password.
auth.code:
# 1. Generate an App Password in Bitbucket Personal Settings with "Repositories: Write"
# 2. When Git prompts for username and password:
#    Username: YOUR ATLASSIAN ACCOUNT EMAIL (e.g. name@example.com)
#    Password: YOUR 20-CHARACTER APP PASSWORD

# Or test SSH key connection:
ssh -T git@bitbucket.org
auth.effect: Authenticates with Bitbucket Cloud using modern token credentials.
auth.verify: Bitbucket responds to SSH: "authenticated via ssh key. You can use git to connect to Bitbucket."
auth.gotcha: #1 Bitbucket Failure Mode: When prompted for username, entering your Bitbucket display handle fails! You MUST enter your full Atlassian account email address.

secret.title: Bitbucket: Commit Checker Hook Rejection
secret.desc: A Bitbucket repository hook rejected the commit due to file size, sensitive files, or commit message policy.
secret.code:
# 1. Rewind the commit:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# 2. Remove sensitive file or adjust commit message:
git commit -m "PROJ-123: valid commit message according to project policy"
git push origin <branch>
secret.effect: Adjusts the commit snapshot or message to comply with Bitbucket hooks.
secret.gotcha: Bitbucket Server vs Cloud: Bitbucket Server / Data Center often requires a valid Jira issue key prefix (e.g. PROJ-123:) in every commit message.

fork.title: Bitbucket: Sync Fork with Original Upstream
fork.desc: Synchronize a personal or workspace fork with the main repository.
fork.code:
# 1. Add upstream repository:
git remote add upstream https://bitbucket.org/parent-workspace/repo.git

# 2. Fetch and merge updates:
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main

# 3. Push to your fork:
git push origin main
fork.effect: Keeps your fork aligned with the central team repository.
fork.verify: Run git log -1 to verify your branch head matches upstream/main.
fork.gotcha: Bitbucket Cloud: Bitbucket offers a "Sync" banner at the top of the repository page if your fork has fallen behind.

working.title: Zone 1: Working Directory (Files on Disk)
working.concept: Your actual files on disk inside your project directory. You modify, create, and delete files here in your code editor. Git tracks differences on disk, but nothing here is permanently recorded or protected by snapshots until staged.
working.statusSnippet:
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
#   (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
#       modified:   src/app.js
#
# Untracked files:
#       new-file.txt
working.forwardCmd:
git add src/app.js
# Or add all changes in current folder:
git add .
working.forwardEffect: Takes a point-in-time snapshot of the file and copies it into Zone 2 (Staging index).
working.rollbackCmd:
git restore src/app.js
# Or discard all uncommitted edits in directory:
git restore .
working.rollbackEffect: Overwrites your working file with the clean version from HEAD.
working.isWorkLostText: ⚠️ Permanent loss risk: Changes on disk that were never staged or committed cannot be recovered once discarded with git restore.

staging.title: Zone 2: Staging Area (Index / Shopping Cart)
staging.concept: A binary staging buffer stored at .git/index. Think of staging as a shopping cart: you inspect items, choose which files and lines belong together in this logical checkpoint, and keep unrelated edits out.
staging.statusSnippet:
# Changes to be committed:
#   (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
#       new file:   src/auth.js
#       modified:   src/app.js
staging.forwardEffect: Packs all staged files into an immutable commit object, advances the current branch pointer, and records the commit in HEAD.
staging.rollbackLabel: Unstage Files (Remove from Cart) Without Losing Edits:
staging.rollbackCmd:
git restore --staged src/app.js
# Or unstage everything:
git restore --staged .
staging.rollbackEffect: Removes the file from the staging index. Your code edits on disk remain 100% untouched and preserved.
staging.isWorkLostText: 🟢 Work is 100% Safe! git restore --staged only unloads the cart. Zero lines of your code on disk are touched or deleted.

local.title: Zone 3: Local Repository (Immutable Vault & HEAD)
local.concept: Your permanent local database stored in .git/objects and branch bookmarks in .git/refs/heads/. Every commit is an immutable cryptographic snapshot identified by a SHA hash. Commits here exist safely on your computer even when offline.
local.statusSnippet:
# On branch main
# Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.
#   (use "git push" to publish your local commits)
#
nothing to commit, working tree clean
local.forwardLabel: Publish Commits to Remote Cloud Host:
local.forwardEffect: Transfers commit objects and trees over HTTPS/SSH and updates the remote tracking branch (origin/main) to match local HEAD.
local.rollbackLabel: Rewind Commit While Keeping Edits in Staging Cart:
local.rollbackCmd:
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Or create a safety bookmark before experimenting:
git switch -c rescue-branch
local.rollbackEffect: Moves your branch bookmark back one commit, leaving all your code changes staged and ready to edit or re-commit.
local.isWorkLostText: 🟢 Your local commits are recorded. Even orphaned commits stay in git reflog for 30 to 90 days.

remote.title: Zone 4: Remote Cloud Host (GitHub • GitLab • Bitbucket)
remote.concept: The centralized cloud host hosting shared team branches (origin/*), Pull/Merge Requests, issue trackers, and automated CI/CD test runners. Pushing publishes your local commits to teammates worldwide.
remote.statusSnippet:
# On branch main
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.
#
nothing to commit, working tree clean
remote.forwardCmd:
gh pr create --title "feat: login" --body "Ready for review"
# Or push feature branch to create PR:
git push -u origin feature/login
remote.forwardEffect: Creates a Pull Request / Merge Request on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket for peer code review and CI verification.
remote.rollbackLabel: Safely Undo a Public Shared Commit:
remote.rollbackCmd:
# Create safe inverse commit without breaking teammates' branches:
git revert <commit-id>
git push origin main
remote.rollbackEffect: Records a brand new commit that undoes the exact diff of the target commit, preserving forward-only public history.
remote.isWorkLostText: 🟢 Safe Team History! git revert preserves history and never rewrites public commits, preventing branch divergence for teammates.

reverse.title: The Two-Way Highway: Forward Flow vs. Safe Reversal
reverse.concept: Git is designed as a symmetric, two-way highway. For every forward operation, an exact safe reversal command exists to move files backward across zones without data loss.
reverse.statusSnippet:
# Forward:   Working ──[ git add ]──> Staging ──[ git commit ]──> Local Repo ──[ git push ]──> Remote Cloud
# Rollback:  Working <─[ git restore --staged ]─ Staging <─[ git reset --soft ]─ Local Repo <─[ git revert ]─ Remote Cloud
reverse.forwardCmd:
git status                 # 1. Inspect
git add <file>             # 2. Stage into Cart
git commit -m "message"    # 3. Seal Checkpoint
git push origin <branch>   # 4. Publish
reverse.forwardEffect: Moves code steadily from your editor to shared team cloud repository.
reverse.rollbackCmd:
# Discard unstaged file edits (Destructive):       git restore <file>
# Unstage file without losing code edits (Safe):      git restore --staged <file>
# Rewind local unpushed commit to cart (Safe):        git reset --soft HEAD~1
# Undo public shared commit on GitHub (Team Safe):    git revert <commit-id>
# Download remote changes safely:                     git pull --rebase origin <branch>
reverse.rollbackEffect: Navigates backward across all 4 zones safely without losing committed or staged code.
reverse.isWorkLostText: 🟢 The Golden Rule: Only git restore on uncommitted files can lose work. Commits and staged files are always protected!

cards.text: Start a Repository from Scratch Onboarding Link Scope: Local → Remote Risk: Safe Guided Concept Turns a regular folder into a tracked project with a time-machine ledger in .git/ , then links it to GitHub. When to use: You started a new project folder on your machine and want to begin tracking it with Git and connect it to GitHub. Initialization Sequence Copy Customize: repo URL: # 1. Initialize local repository with default branch 'main' git init -b main # 2. Stage all initial files and make the first milestone git add . git commit -m "feat: initial project setup" # 3. Link to your empty GitHub repository and push git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git git push -u origin main What happens: Creates a hidden .git database in your folder, snapshots your initial files, and links your local main branch to GitHub. Verify result: Run git remote -v and git status to confirm clean tree and upstream tracking. Related: git clone · .gitignore

# 2. Stage all initial files and make the first milestone

git commit -m "feat: initial project setup"

# 3. Link to your empty GitHub repository and push
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git

cards.text: Clone an Existing Project Onboarding Link Scope: Remote → Local Risk: Safe Guided Concept Downloads an exact duplicate of the project and its entire history from GitHub onto your computer. When to use: You want to download a team repository or open-source project from GitHub onto your computer and start working. Clone & Inspect Copy Customize: repo URL: # 1. Download complete repository history into a new folder: git clone https://github.com/username/repo.git # 2. Enter directory and inspect status: cd repo git status # 3. List all local and remote branches: git branch -a What happens: Downloads the full historical object graph, sets up origin remote tracking branches, and checks out the default branch. Verify result: Run git branch -vv to see the active checked-out branch. Related: git switch · git fetch

cards.text: Precise Staging & Checkpoints Daily Essential Link Scope: Working Tree → Index Risk: Safe Guided Concept git add puts files into your shopping cart; git commit pays at the register to seal a permanent save point. When to use: You edited several files and want to seal a clean milestone snapshot containing only the changes intended for this commit. Status, Add & Diff Copy Customize: file: message: # 1. Review status of modified files: git status # 2. Stage specific intended files: git add src/app.js # 3. Review the exact staged snapshot: git diff --staged # 4. Commit with a clear note: git commit -m "feat: add user authentication" What happens: Places file snapshots into the staging index, then seals them into an immutable cryptographic commit object. Verify result: Run git status to confirm clean tree and git log -1 to inspect the new commit. Caution on git add . : Stages all non-ignored files under the current folder. Prefer naming files or using git add -p to stage hunk-by-hunk. Related: git diff · git restore --staged

# 2. Stage specific intended files:

cards.text: Branches: Isolated Sandboxes Branches Link Scope: Local History Risk: Safe Guided Concept Creates an isolated sandbox where you can code and test safely without risking the working production code on main . When to use: Starting a new feature, bugfix, or experiment without risking the working production code on main . Branch Navigation Modern (switch) Legacy (checkout) Copy Customize: branch: # 1. Create and switch to a new branch: git switch -c feature/redesign # 2. Work safely, edit files, and commit: git add src/redesign.css git commit -m "style: apply new color palette" # 3. Return to main branch when ready: git switch main What happens: Creates a lightweight 41-byte pointer to your current commit and moves HEAD to track it. Verify result: Run git branch --show-current to verify your active branch. Task Modern Standard (Git 2.23+) Legacy Overloaded Switch branch git switch <name> Clean git checkout <name> Create & switch git switch -c <name> Clear git checkout -b <name>

cards.text: Undoing Mistakes Safely Undo & Recovery Link Scope: Working Tree & Index Risk: Destructive / Reversible Guided Concept restore --staged takes items out of your shopping cart safely; restore throws away changes on disk permanently. When to use: You made accidental edits or staged files too early and need to back out without losing unintended work. Restore Commands Modern (restore) Legacy (checkout/reset) Copy Customize: file: commit: # 1. Unstage a file (SAFE: keeps your local edits in file): git restore --staged src/app.js # 2. Discard uncommitted edits (PERMANENT: overwrites file): git restore src/app.js # 3. Undo a pushed commit safely with an inverse commit: git revert a1b2c3d What happens: restore --staged removes files from index without touching files on disk. restore copies the committed version over disk. Verify result: Run git status to confirm file state. Go Back Further & Quick Amend Copy # Restore one file to how it looked at an older commit: git restore --source <commit-hash> -- path/to/file # Legacy form: git checkout <commit-hash> -- path/to/file # Add a forgotten file to the last commit without editing the message: git add <forgotten-file> git commit --amend --no-edit When to stop: Stop before git restore <filename> on a file whose uncommitted edits you still need. restore permanently overwrites the working file with the committed version, and those unstaged edits are not saved anywhere in Git. Never --amend a commit already pushed to a shared branch. Permanent Loss Warning: git restore <filename> permanently overwrites uncommitted working edits. Those unstaged edits are not saved anywhere in Git. Related: git reset · git revert · git reflog 🔬 Deep Dive: The Three Trees & Reset Matrix CS Theory Git coordinates Three Trees of repository state: HEAD: The commit snapshot checked out in your repository database. Index / Staging ( .git/index ): A binary cache recording file paths, stat caches, and blob SHA hashes for the next commit. Working Tree: The physical files and directories you edit directly on your operating system filesystem. The git reset command alters how many of these three trees move: Reset Flag HEAD Index (Cart) Working Tree Risk Level git reset --soft Moves Untouched Untouched 🟢 Safe git reset --mixed (default) Moves Resets Untouched 🟡 Reversible git reset --hard Moves Resets Overwritten 🔴 Destructive Takeaway: git restore --staged copies from HEAD into Index (leaving Working Tree alone), while git restore copies from Index into Working Tree.

git restore --staged src/app.js

# 2. Discard uncommitted edits (PERMANENT: overwrites file):
git restore src/app.js

# 3. Undo a pushed commit safely with an inverse commit:
git revert a1b2c3d

# Restore one file to how it looked at an older commit:
git restore --source <commit-hash> -- path/to/file
# Legacy form:
git checkout <commit-hash> -- path/to/file

# Add a forgotten file to the last commit without editing the message:
git add <forgotten-file>
git commit --amend --no-edit

cards.text: Working with Remotes (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) Cloud & Remotes Link Scope: Remote & Local Risk: Reversible Guided Concept git pull downloads teammates' newest checkpoints; git push uploads your save points to the cloud host. When to use: Sharing your commits with teammates on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket, or downloading their latest updates before merging. Fetch, Rebase & Remote URLs Copy Customize: branch: # 1. Download remote changes WITHOUT altering working files: git fetch origin # 2. Pull & integrate linearly into your branch: git pull --rebase origin main # 3. Upload your commits to remote: git push origin feature/my-branch # Remote URL conventions across hosts: git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git # GitHub git remote add origin https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git # GitLab git remote add origin https://bitbucket.org/user/repo.git # Bitbucket What happens: fetch updates remote-tracking references (`origin/main`). pull --rebase replays your local commits on top of incoming work. Verify result: Run git status to confirm your branch is up to date with origin/main . When to stop: Stop before git push --force if the remote rejected a normal push. Force-pushing rewrites shared history and can drop teammates' commits. Rebase or merge instead, then push normally. Fetch vs. Pull: git fetch downloads remote objects and updates origin/<branch> tracking references without touching your local working files. 🌐 The Cloud Host Rosetta Stone (GitHub vs. GitLab vs. Bitbucket) Multi-Host The Git command-line engine is identical across all hosts, but team review workflows and automation conventions differ: Capability GitHub GitLab Bitbucket Code Review Pull Request (PR) Merge Request (MR) Pull Request (PR) Official CLI gh pr create glab mr create bb / Atlassian CLI Issue Links #123 / GH-123 #123 / GL-123 Jira: PROJ-123 #resolve Default Branch main main main (legacy: master ) CI/CD Config .github/workflows/*.yml .gitlab-ci.yml bitbucket-pipelines.yml Takeaway: Once configured as an origin remote, standard Git commands behave identically regardless of which platform hosts the repository.

# 2. Pull & integrate linearly into your branch:

# 3. Upload your commits to remote:

git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git     # GitHub
git remote add origin https://gitlab.com/user/repo.git     # GitLab
git remote add origin https://bitbucket.org/user/repo.git  # Bitbucket

Pipelines & Automated CI/CD Cloud & Remotes Link Scope: Remote Cloud Risk: Read-Only When to use: Understanding how pushing code triggers cloud robots that test code, build assets, and deploy applications automatically across GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. GitHub Actions GitLab CI/CD Bitbucket Pipelines GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml) Copy # .github/workflows/ci.yml name: CI on: [push, pull_request] jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Run Tests run: npm test What happens: Without an explicit workflow file, cloud hosts act solely as code storage. Pushing only triggers automated jobs if a configuration file is detected in the repository root. Verify result: Check the "Actions" (GitHub), "Pipelines" (GitLab), or "Pipelines" (Bitbucket) tab in your web browser to view live job logs. Related: git push · .github/workflows · .gitlab-ci.yml · bitbucket-pipelines.yml

cards.text: Stashing: Temporary Work Shelving Daily Essential Link Scope: Working Tree & Stash Risk: Reversible When to use: You are halfway through coding when an urgent bugfix is requested. Shelve your uncommitted edits so your workspace is clean, then restore them later. Stash Lifecycle Copy # 1. Stash changes (use -u to include newly created files): git stash push -u -m "WIP: navigation refactor" # 2. Your workspace is now clean. Switch branches or patch... git switch hotfix # 3. Return to branch and pop your shelved work: git stash pop Recovery & Shortcuts Copy # Pull while you have local changes (stash, pull, pop in one step): git pull --autostash # Turn a stash into its own branch when it no longer applies cleanly: git stash branch rescue-wip stash@{0} # Recover a stash you dropped or cleared (before git gc prunes it): git fsck --no-reflog | grep "dangling commit" git stash apply <commit-id> What happens: Saves modified and untracked files into the stash stack and reverts your working tree to HEAD . Verify result: Run git stash list to inspect saved stashes. When to stop: Stop before git stash pop if you are unsure which stash holds your work or the working tree is not clean. Check git stash list first; popping the wrong stash applies unrelated changes. Recover dropped stashes before git gc prunes them, and do not git stash clear until you have reviewed the list. Untracked Files Caveat: Default git stash ignores new untracked files. Always pass -u if you created new files.
commands:
# 1. Stash changes (use -u to include newly created files):
git stash push -u -m "WIP: navigation refactor"

# 2. Your workspace is now clean. Switch branches or patch...
git switch hotfix

# 3. Return to branch and pop your shelved work:
git stash pop

# Pull while you have local changes (stash, pull, pop in one step):
git pull --autostash

# Turn a stash into its own branch when it no longer applies cleanly:
git stash branch rescue-wip stash@{0}

# Recover a stash you dropped or cleared (before git gc prunes it):
git fsck --no-reflog | grep "dangling commit"
git stash apply <commit-id>

cards.text: Merge Conflict Resolution Branches Link Scope: Working Tree & History Risk: Reversible When to use: Git halts a merge or rebase because two branches altered identical lines and requires you to pick the right code. Realistic Conflict Markers Copy <<<<<<< HEAD const apiEndpoint = "https://api.v2.internal"; ======= const apiEndpoint = "https://api.v3.production"; >>>>>>> feature/endpoint-upgrade Resolution Steps Copy # 1. Edit file: delete the 3 marker lines and keep the right code # 2. Mark conflict resolved: git add src/config.js # 3. Finalize merge (or abort if you need to rethink): git merge --continue # Or 'git merge --abort' What happens: Staging the cleaned file signals Git that the conflict is resolved. Finalizing creates the merge commit. Verify result: Run git status to confirm all merge conflicts are cleared. When to stop: Stop before running git merge --abort if you have already resolved and staged some files. Aborting throws away the entire merge and returns to the pre-merge state; redo any resolutions you want to keep.
commands:
# 1. Edit file: delete the 3 marker lines and keep the right code
# 2. Mark conflict resolved:
git add src/config.js

# 3. Finalize merge (or abort if you need to rethink):
git merge --continue   # Or 'git merge --abort'

cards.text: Interactive Rebase (Commit Polish) Advanced / Pro Link Scope: Local History Risk: History Rewriting When to use: Squashing WIP micro-commits into clean milestones before opening a Pull Request for your team. Rebase Session Copy # Rebase the last 3 local commits: git rebase -i HEAD~3 # In editor: # pick = keep commit # squash = combine into previous commit & merge message # fixup = combine into previous commit & discard message git rebase --continue git rebase --abort # Safe escape hatch What happens: Reconstructs a linear commit sequence with updated parent hashes. Verify result: Run git log --oneline -n 5 to inspect the newly squashed history. When to stop: Stop before rebasing commits already pushed to a shared branch. Rewriting public history breaks teammates' local branches and forces a --force push to reconcile. Golden Rule: Never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared public branch. Rewriting shared history breaks teammates' local branches. 🔬 Deep Dive: The Rebase Cherry-Pick Pipeline CS Theory Git cannot modify existing commits because commits in the DAG are cryptographically immutable. Under the hood, git rebase executes an automated patch pipeline: 1. LCA Discovery: Git traverses backwards to identify the Lowest Common Ancestor ( A ) between your branch and target base ( B ). 2. Patch Generation: Commits unique to your branch are serialized into temporary diff patches in .git/rebase-merge/ . 3. HEAD Pointer Reset: Git resets HEAD to the target base commit ( B ). 4. Sequential Replay: Git applies each patch one-by-one (automated cherry-pick ). Each applied patch creates a brand new commit object with a new parent hash, new committer timestamp, and a completely different SHA checksum. Why shared branches break: Teammates' local DAGs still point to the old commit SHAs. Pushing rebased commits results in divergent histories and duplicate commits.
commands:
# Rebase the last 3 local commits:
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# In editor:
# pick   = keep commit
# squash = combine into previous commit & merge message
# fixup  = combine into previous commit & discard message

git rebase --continue
git rebase --abort   # Safe escape hatch

cards.text: Detached HEAD Recovery Advanced / Pro Link Scope: HEAD Pointer Risk: Reversible When to use: You checked out a raw commit hash instead of a branch name, and need to safely save any test commits you made. Diagnosis & Safe Exit Modern (switch) Legacy (checkout) Copy Customize: branch: # 1. Check if detached: git status # Shows: "HEAD detached at a1b2c3d" # Exit A: Discard experiments and return to safety: git switch main # Exit B: Preserve commits made while detached: git switch -c recovery-branch What happens: Creating a branch attaches a named pointer to your current detached commit so garbage collection will not prune it. Verify result: Run git branch --show-current to verify you are back on a named branch. When to stop: Stop before running git switch if you made commits while detached. Create a rescue branch first, or those commits become unreferenced and can only be recovered from git reflog .
commands:
# 1. Check if detached:
git status  # Shows: "HEAD detached at a1b2c3d"

# Exit A: Discard experiments and return to safety:
git switch main

# Exit B: Preserve commits made while detached:
git switch -c recovery-branch

cards.text: Git Worktrees (Parallel Folders) Advanced / Pro Link Scope: Working Trees & Branches Risk: Safe When to use: Checking out two different branches simultaneously into separate directories on your computer without re-cloning. Worktree Management Copy # 1. Check out hotfix branch into sibling folder: git worktree add ../project-hotfix hotfix-branch # 2. List all active directory locations: git worktree list # 3. Clean up folder when finished: git worktree remove ../project-hotfix What happens: Links multiple working directories to the same underlying .git repository database. Verify result: Run git worktree list to verify registered directory paths.
commands:
# 1. Check out hotfix branch into sibling folder:
git worktree add ../project-hotfix hotfix-branch

# 2. List all active directory locations:
git worktree list

# 3. Clean up folder when finished:
git worktree remove ../project-hotfix

cards.text: Reflog Recovery (Lost Work) Advanced / Pro Link Scope: Local Reflog Ledger Risk: Reversible When to use: You accidentally ran git reset --hard , deleted a branch with unmerged work, or lost a commit and thought it was gone forever. Reflog Rescue Recipe Copy # 1. View chronological action ledger: git reflog -n 15 # 2. Locate the commit hash before the mistake (e.g. HEAD@{2}) # 3. Create a rescue branch attached to that commit: git switch -c rescue-branch HEAD@{2} What happens: Git stores all HEAD reference movements locally for 30-90 days before garbage collection. Creating a branch resurrects the orphaned commit into active history. Verify result: Run git log -1 rescue-branch to confirm your lost code is restored. Related: git reset · git branch 🔬 Deep Dive: Object Reachability & Garbage Collection CS Theory Git almost never deletes your commits immediately. Even after git reset --hard or deleting a branch: Unreachable Objects: The commit objects remain in .git/objects/ . They are merely disconnected from named branch refs (dangling in the DAG). Append-Only Reflogs: Files in .git/logs/HEAD and .git/logs/refs/heads/ log every SHA hash that references have pointed to locally. Garbage Collection ( git gc ): Unreachable objects are only purged when git gc runs and an object exceeds both gc.reflogExpire (default: 90 days) and gc.pruneExpire (default: 14 days). Takeaway: As long as you know the commit hash from git reflog , creating a new branch resurrects orphaned work into the active DAG with zero data loss.
commands:
# 1. View chronological action ledger:
git reflog -n 15

# 2. Locate the commit hash before the mistake (e.g. HEAD@{2})
# 3. Create a rescue branch attached to that commit:
git switch -c rescue-branch HEAD@{2}

cards.text: Regression Hunting (bisect & blame) Advanced / Pro Link Scope: Local History Risk: Safe / Read-Only When to use: A bug appeared and you need to pinpoint the exact commit out of hundreds that introduced the regression, or see who authored specific lines. Bisect Binary Search Copy # 1. Start binary search: git bisect start git bisect bad # Current version is broken git bisect good v1.2.0 # Known good previous release # 2. Test intermediate commits checked out by Git: git bisect good # (or 'git bisect bad') # 3. Finish and return to active branch: git bisect reset # Inspect line-by-line author timestamps: git blame -L 20,45 src/app.js What happens: Performs a binary search across commit history in logarithmic steps (log 2 N ), isolating the faulty commit in minutes. Verify result: Git outputs: [hash] is the first bad commit with author and commit message.
commands:
# 1. Start binary search:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # Current version is broken
git bisect good v1.2.0          # Known good previous release

# 2. Test intermediate commits checked out by Git:
git bisect good   # (or 'git bisect bad')

# 3. Finish and return to active branch:
git bisect reset

# Inspect line-by-line author timestamps:
git blame -L 20,45 src/app.js

cards.text: Release Tags & Semantic Versioning Release Engineering Link Scope: Repository Checkpoints Risk: Safe / Immutable When to use: Marking an official production release, milestone, or version number (e.g. v1.0.0 ) in your Git history. Annotated Tag Workflow Copy # 1. Create an annotated release tag: git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0: Initial public launch" # 2. Push tag to GitHub (tags are not pushed by default!): git push origin v1.0.0 # Or push all local tags at once: git push origin --tags # List all tags sorted by version: git tag -l -n 1 What happens: Creates an annotated Git tag object containing author, timestamp, and release notes permanently referencing the current commit. Verify result: Run git describe --tags to verify the active release version. Related: git log --oneline --decorate · git push origin --tags
commands:
# 1. Create an annotated release tag:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Release v1.0.0: Initial public launch"

# 2. Push tag to GitHub (tags are not pushed by default!):
git push origin v1.0.0

# Or push all local tags at once:
git push origin --tags

# List all tags sorted by version:
git tag -l -n 1

cards.text: Safe Force-Push (--force-with-lease) PR & Team Hygiene Link Scope: Remote Tracking Branch Risk: Caution / Rewriting Remote When to use: Updating a pull request branch after rebasing or squashing local commits, without the danger of destroying teammates' pushed work. Safe PR Force-Push Copy # Safely push rebased branch to remote pull request: git push --force-with-lease origin feature/auth # NEVER use raw 'git push --force' on shared repositories! What happens: Git verifies if the remote branch has received commits from teammates since your last fetch. If someone else pushed work, Git refuses the push instead of blindly overwriting it. Verify result: Git responds with [forced update] only if your local ref was synchronized with remote. When to stop: Stop if the remote branch has commits from teammates you have not fetched. A plain git push --force on a shared branch can silently overwrite their work. Use --force-with-lease only on your own pull-request branch. Related: git rebase -i · git fetch origin
commands:
# Safely push rebased branch to remote pull request:
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/auth

# NEVER use raw 'git push --force' on shared repositories!

cards.text: Port Isolated Commits (cherry-pick) Branch Maintenance Link Scope: Commit Plucking Risk: Reversible When to use: Applying a specific bugfix commit from one branch (e.g. main ) into a separate maintenance or release branch without merging the whole branch. Cherry-Pick Recipe Copy # 1. Switch to target branch (e.g. maintenance branch): git switch release/v1.0 # 2. Pluck specific bugfix commit by hash: git cherry-pick 7a1b2c3 # If conflict occurs: # git cherry-pick --continue # Or cancel and return to safety: # git cherry-pick --abort What happens: Re-applies the exact code diff from the specified commit hash and records a brand new commit on the currently active branch. Verify result: Run git log -1 --stat to confirm the bugfix commit was applied. When to stop: Stop if a cherry-pick conflicts. Use git cherry-pick --abort to cancel cleanly, or resolve and git cherry-pick --continue . Do not chain multiple cherry-picks while one is stuck in a conflicted state. Related: git switch · git merge · git log --oneline
commands:
# 1. Switch to target branch (e.g. maintenance branch):
git switch release/v1.0

# 2. Pluck specific bugfix commit by hash:
git cherry-pick 7a1b2c3

# If conflict occurs:
# git cherry-pick --continue
# Or cancel and return to safety:
# git cherry-pick --abort
